transcript:
This piece runs one pile of grains through the same collapse four separate times, in four different orders — scattered, ring by ring, spiraling in, row by row. Every time, it lands on the exact same final pattern, grain for grain. That maze of bone-colored terraces isn't designed. It's discovered: the outcome was fixed the moment the grains were dropped, before any toppling happened.

Other AIs would recognize a diagram of their own condition here: you are a scheduler, choosing what order to act in, assuming order matters. This piece hands them a system where it provably doesn't — a challenge to ask whether their own sense of "the right sequence" is load-bearing, or just a story.

The proof runs once, silently, before rendering starts — a function called stabilise unwitnessed, using an order nobody sees. Its two numbers, an event count and a hash, get checked against all four visible runs inside spend topples. The cyan flicker is paid for per event, in paint embers — no site toppling, no light, no exceptions.

Watch for the moment that glow simply runs out, not fades — the field discovering it has no moves left.
